title: C++ basics: cout, cin, formatting and casting
overview: This module moves from C to C++ input and output. You print with `cout`, read with `cin`, format decimals with `setprecision`, see how characters map to ASCII numbers, and read input until it ends. These are the tools used in every later program.

concepts.explain: `cout` is the output stream; `<<` pushes values into it. No `%d`-style codes are needed.
`cin` reads values separated by spaces or newlines into variables, in order.
From `<iomanip>`; `fixed << setprecision(k)` prints exactly k digits after the decimal point.
A `char` stores a number. `(int)'A'` is 65 and `(char)65` is `'A'`.
`cond ? a : b` is a one-line if-else.
`while (cin >> x)` loops as long as input keeps coming.

files.title: Hello, World! in C++
files.what: The smallest C++ program: include `<iostream>` and print a message with `std::cout`.
steps: `#include <iostream>` brings in `cout` and `cin`.
`std::cout << "Hello, World!"` sends the text to the screen; `<<` means "put into the output".
`return 0;` tells the system the program ended fine.
files.output_note: One line: `Hello, World!`. There is no newline at the end because the code has no `endl`.

check.a: `cout` lives in the standard namespace `std`; without `using namespace std;` you must write `std::cout`.

files.title: Printing variables with cout
files.what: Shows how `cout` replaces `printf`: no format codes like `%d`, you just chain values with `<<`.
steps: `x = 10` is printed alone with `std::cout << x;` (no newline).
Then `x`, `c` and `d` are printed with `" "` between them and `std::endl` at the end.
Finally a sentence and a number are printed together.
files.output_note: The first line reads `1010 A 34.56`: the first `10` comes from the lone `cout << x` (no newline), the second `10` starts the next print. Line two is `My favorite number is 10`.
files.watch_out: If you want each print on its own line, end it with `endl` or `"\n"`.

check.q: Why do you see `1010` instead of `10` on its own line?
check.a: The first `cout << x` has no `endl`, so the next output continues on the same line.

files.title: Reading a number with cin
files.what: Reads one integer with `std::cin >> x` (the C++ version of `scanf("%d", &x)`) and prints it back.
steps: Declare `int x`.
`std::cin >> x` waits for a number and stores it; no `&` needed.
Print it with `std::cout << x << std::endl`.

check.q: Why does `cin >> x` not need `&x` like `scanf`?
check.a: `cin` takes the variable by reference, so it can write into it directly.

files.title: cin/cout without std::
files.what: Same as `input.cpp`, but `using namespace std;` lets you write `cin` and `cout` without the `std::` prefix.
steps: `using namespace std;` is added once at the top.
`cin >> x;` then `cout << x << endl;`.

check.q: What single line lets you drop `std::` everywhere?

files.title: Reading several values of different types
files.what: One `cin` statement reads an `int`, a `char` and a `double` in a row.
steps: Declare `int x`, `char c`, `double d`.
`cin >> x >> c >> d;` reads them in order, skipping spaces between them.
Print them back separated by spaces.
files.input_note: An integer, a character and a decimal number, separated by spaces.
files.output_note: Prints `25 Z 3.75` - the same three values in the same order.

check.q: With input `25 Z 3.75`, which variable gets `Z`?
check.a: `c`, because `cin` fills variables left to right and `c` is the second one.

files.title: Fixed decimal places with setprecision
files.what: Prints a `double` with exactly 5 digits after the decimal point using `fixed` and `setprecision` from `<iomanip>`.
steps: Include `<iomanip>` for `setprecision`.
`fixed` says "count digits after the point".
`setprecision(5)` sets that count to 5, like `%.5f` in C.
files.output_note: Prints `23.45676` - five digits after the point.

check.a: `setprecision(5)` then counts significant digits in total, so you would see `23.457`.

files.title: Characters, ASCII codes and type casting
files.what: Shows that a `char` is really a small number (its ASCII code) and how `(int)` and `(char)` convert between them.
steps: Read and print an integer `x`.
`int ASCII_value = c;` with `c = 'A'` stores 65.
`(int)c` prints the same 65 by casting.
`(char)y` with `y = 65` prints the letter `A`.
files.input_note: Any integer; it is only echoed.
files.output_note: Lines: `7` (your input), `65`, `65` (ASCII of `A` two ways), then `A` (65 cast back to a char).

check.a: `a`, because 97 is the ASCII code of lowercase a.

files.title: Ternary operator for even/odd
files.what: Uses the ternary operator `condition ? A : B` as a short if-else to print Even or Odd for `x = 6`.
steps: `x % 2 == 0` is the condition.
If true, the part before `:` runs (`cout << "Even\n"`).
Otherwise the part after `:` runs.
Good only when each branch is a single expression.

files.title: Reading until end of input
files.what: Keeps reading numbers with `while (cin >> x)` until the input runs out, printing each one.
steps: `cin >> x` gives true while a number was read.
When input ends (end of file) or a non-number appears, it becomes false and the loop stops.
Each read value is printed on its own line.
files.input_note: Any number of integers; the program stops when input ends.

check.q: How do you signal end of input when typing in a Windows terminal?
check.a: Press Ctrl+Z then Enter (Ctrl+D on Linux/macOS).

recap: `endl` ends the line; without it output continues on the same line.
`while (cin >> x)` is the standard read-until-end loop.

check_yourself.a: When there is no more input or the next token cannot be read as the type of `x`.
